name: Kira Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the haul truck at a large mine, usually moving rock from the west ramp to the crusher. I joined mining later than most and am still a junior operator, so I ask questions when a warning light catches me out. I like the early light over the pit; I don't like how a long shift makes my knees ache.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the machine has its uses, but the haul trucks still need people watching the ground. I use an AI assistant on my phone every day to explain unfamiliar dashboard warnings, then I check the manual and ask our fitter before touching anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A flat AI future wouldn't settle my own money question. I came into mining late and I'm still junior at 58, so one repair bill could eat a good share of the three months of expenses we have saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my truck shift and keep logging the warning codes I don't recognise. Starting now, I'd transfer a small sum after each payday into our repair account; in the first year of a plateau, I'd do the same and ask the trainer to check my reversing on the west ramp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly steady about the machines and less steady about my knees. My partner Farid and I can pay the bills while I'm working, but neither of us calls three months of savings a retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What made you cautious about the warning light?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month an amber light came on halfway down the west ramp, and I parked instead of trusting the phone. The fitter found a loose sensor, which is why I still want a person to sign off on a fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the savings have to cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown son lives on his own now, so we aren't paying school costs. The expense I keep thinking about is the roof over our kitchen, because a leak would take cash we meant for retirement.

say: When AI is **minor**, I would still want a fitter to check faults before equipment moves.
Our **three-month cushion** makes me cautious even if the job itself stays much the same.
think: I worry that **one repair** could consume our three-month cushion before retirement.
My **late start** means I still need the ordinary mining wage.
do: Keep **truck shifts** and log unfamiliar fault codes for a fitter.
Transfer **payday money** to the roof account and ask for reversing feedback.
feel: **Steady** about machinery, but uneasy about aching knees and retirement money.
S0.quote: I use an AI assistant on my phone every day to explain unfamiliar dashboard warnings, then I check the manual and ask our fitter before touching anything.
fieldNote: Kira treats **phone advice** as a prompt to check equipment, never as clearance to operate it.
Her present worry comes from a **late start** in mining, limited savings and a likely roof repair, not AI alone.

steps.text: Keep working haul-truck shifts and log unfamiliar warning codes
Transfer a small sum after each payday into the roof repair account
Ask the fitter for feedback on reversing the truck

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office will feel this first: buying, rosters and reports can move into software before a robot touches a truck. I'd ask the crew to watch for fewer trainee places, because that tells us more than a glossy demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm curious about the tools, but I know I'm still one of the least experienced drivers on the roster. If a computer plans shorter routes and management needs fewer shifts, my typical wage and our roof fund both suffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask the trainer for a supervised session with the new dispatch screen and use my phone assistant to practise the terms afterward. If the change arrived over the next few years, I'd apply for an equipment inspection trainee opening at this mine and at two nearby mines, while keeping my driving shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes me alert rather than frozen. Learning a screen is possible for me, but an inspection opening isn't a promise and I cannot retire on a short savings account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider a dispatch-room transfer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I used to think the dispatch room was a safe place to move my body out of a truck. Once I saw route suggestions appear on our tablets, I stopped treating a desk transfer as an escape route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change at home if hours fell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show our grown daughter the actual shift roster, not make a speech about technology. Farid and I would hold off replacing the sofa if overtime dropped, because that purchase can wait and the roof cannot.

say: I would say **office tasks** change first and ask whether the mine is still taking trainees.
I would ask the crew to watch for **fewer trainee places** instead of trusting glossy demonstrations.
think: I fear **shorter routes** could mean fewer shifts for junior drivers.
My **curiosity** will not create an inspection vacancy by itself.
do: Practise **dispatch terms** with a trainer and phone assistant this month.
Apply for **inspection trainee** openings at three mines while driving shifts continue.
feel: **Alert**, but worried that learning may not secure a new opening.
S1.quote: I used to think the dispatch room was a safe place to move my body out of a truck.
fieldNote: She separates software's near-term effect on **dispatch** from the later spread of robots into truck work.
Her early adoption sits beside a practical fear: an **inspection role** may have few openings locally.

steps.text: Practise dispatch terms on the mine screen with a trainer
Apply for equipment inspection trainee openings at three mines
Keep driving scheduled haul-truck shifts while applying
Delay replacing the household sofa if overtime falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my crew that full thinking AI by 2028 could take the planning office quickly, and hands-on robots around 2031 put the truck seats at risk. I'd want clear notices about which machines are being tested and who still has paid shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 60, I couldn't just wait for retirement if the driving work vanished at 63. I'm a junior operator with some nearby mines, but those mines may buy the same robots, so another gate badge might not mean another wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd ask the training office for the requirements to inspect brakes and tyres, then apply for the next supervised place if it opens. In the first year after 2028, I'd keep driving paid shifts, apply for inspection posts at the nearby mines, and put any overtime into the roof account before robots reach the pit around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The short clock makes my stomach tight. I can learn a checklist, but I can't turn two years into a long career or assume inspection stays human once the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you and Farid talked about using the savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Farid asked whether we should use the savings to replace the roof at once. I said we need an estimate first, because spending our whole cushion before we know the price would leave us naked if shifts stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would inspection training really protect you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the mine offered a paid inspection placement, I would take it even if the first few weeks felt embarrassing. I wouldn't call it a secure new trade; robots could inspect as well as drive by 2031.

say: I would warn that **thinking AI in 2028** threatens the planning office before robots reach trucks around 2031.
I would ask for **clear notices** about machine tests and which workers still have paid shifts.
think: I cannot **wait for retirement** if driving wages vanish at 63.
My **nearby mines** might adopt the same robots, leaving fewer alternative wages.
do: Ask about **brake inspection** requirements and seek a paid placement if offered.
Apply for **inspection posts** while keeping paid truck shifts after 2028.
Put **overtime** into the roof account before robots arrive around 2031.
feel: **Tight-stomached** by the short clock and the limits of inspection training.
S2.quote: I'm a junior operator with some nearby mines, but those mines may buy the same robots, so another gate badge might not mean another wage.
fieldNote: The **two-year warning** arrives before Kira can build a larger cushion or a long second career.
She seeks paid inspection training but recognises that **robotic inspection** may follow robotic driving around 2031.

steps.text: Apply for the next paid brake and tyre inspection placement if offered
Apply for inspection posts at nearby mines after 2028
Keep driving paid haul-truck shifts while places remain
Put any overtime into the roof account before 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell people five years is enough time to ask harder questions, but it isn't a guarantee of work. The planners could be displaced when thinking AI arrives in 2031; the robot truck problem comes around 2034, when I'd be 66.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My first thought is that I might reach normal retirement age, but normal age doesn't pay a bill by itself. Farid and I have a modest cushion, no pension figure we can rely on, and I still need wages until we know our actual numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd book an appointment this winter to list our savings, expected bills and whatever retirement entitlement is real, then keep driving and build the repair account. If AGI arrived in 2031, I'd ask for a paid equipment inspection place and apply to the two nearby mines before robots spread around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more room to breathe than in the two-year picture. I also feel a bit foolish admitting how little I know about the money we'd have at 66, so checking it is the first step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughter about retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My daughter once asked when I'd finally put my feet up, and I changed the subject. I don't want to make her our backup plan just because I haven't opened the retirement statement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire before the robots if you could?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the numbers showed we could stop safely before 2034, Farid and I might choose that. Until then I would treat every driving shift as income and every inspection application as a chance, not a promise.

say: I would say **five years** gives us time to check our options before robot trucks arrive around 2034.
I privately need **real retirement figures** before treating age 66 as a safe exit.
think: I need **retirement figures** before believing we can stop driving at 66.
Our **modest cushion** cannot replace wages just because 2034 sounds close to retirement.
do: List **savings and bills** with Farid this winter and keep paid shifts.
Apply for a **paid inspection** place if offered after 2031.
Apply to **two nearby mines** before robots spread around 2034.
feel: More **breathing room**, mixed with embarrassment about unknown retirement income.
S3.quote: My daughter once asked when I'd finally put my feet up, and I changed the subject.
fieldNote: The 2034 robot date meets Kira at 66, close to retirement but without **verified income**.
She wants concrete **household figures** before deciding whether fewer paid shifts are bearable.

steps.text: Keep driving paid shifts through the 2031 planning change
Build the roof repair account with small payday transfers
Apply for a paid equipment inspection place if offered
Apply to two nearby mines for inspection work after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that a decade lets us plan, but full thinking AI in 2036 still has teeth. The office jobs change first; around 2039 robots could take the truck work when I'm 71.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 in 2036, I may have stopped driving, or I may still need the pay. I can't promise a retirement date from a calendar, and I wouldn't tell younger drivers that the robot risk ends with my last shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd get the roof priced and check our retirement figures with Farid, then set a monthly amount we can actually save. If AGI arrived in 2036, I'd review our income before taking more driving shifts; through the first year I'd keep the paid work we need and share the mine's training notices with younger drivers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one feels manageable for my own household if the numbers work. I still feel protective of the crew: a 30-year-old driver can't solve a 2039 robot fleet by waiting to turn 71.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the crew would feel this most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The last time our truck sat idle, the youngest driver had to chase a replacement shift. I could take the delay better than he could, and I hope management remembers whose rent depends on a full roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are you counting on retiring before 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might retire before the robotic fleet if the figures allow it, but I won't spend the savings in advance. Farid and I have learned that a roof estimate can change the whole conversation in one afternoon.

say: I would tell younger drivers that **2039 robots** threaten their truck work even if I have left by then.
My own **retirement date** depends on verified income, not on turning 68 in 2036.
think: I may still need **paid shifts** at 68 despite a decade to prepare.
My **younger colleagues** face a longer robot risk than I do.
do: Price the **kitchen roof** and set a realistic monthly savings amount.
Keep **necessary shifts** through 2037 and share training notices with younger drivers.
feel: **Manageable** for my household if the figures work, but protective of younger crew.
S4.quote: I can't promise a retirement date from a calendar, and I wouldn't tell younger drivers that the robot risk ends with my last shift.
fieldNote: Kira has time to prepare by 2036, yet her present **three-month cushion** still keeps work and money uncertain.
Her concern broadens to **younger operators** whose earning years stretch past the 2039 robot date.

steps.text: Set a monthly savings amount after pricing the kitchen roof
Keep necessary paid driving shifts through the first year after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because the planning office changes when I'm 60 and robot trucks could arrive when I'm 63. A paid inspection placement, honest shift notices and a clear account of our retirement income would help me make choices before we lose wages.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how the mine chooses who gets training. A junior woman who came to the pit late can be curious and quick with a screen and still be last on the list.

headlineQuote: A junior woman who came to the pit late can be curious and quick with a screen and still be last on the list.
portrait: Kira is a **58-year-old junior** haul-truck operator who entered mining late and uses an AI phone assistant daily.
She checks unfamiliar faults with a **fitter**, because she will not let phone advice clear a truck to move.
She and Farid have **three months** of expenses saved and a possible roof repair competing with retirement savings.
She seeks **paid inspection training** while recognising robots could reach both driving and inspection by 2031.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because thinking work changes at 60 and robot trucks could arrive when she is 63.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid inspection place**, honest shift notices and verified retirement income would let her plan before wages disappear.
